reels.title: Code without servers
reels.body: AWS Lambda runs your code without you managing servers. You upload a function; AWS handles the machines, patching and scaling.

reels.title: It runs when something happens
reels.body: Lambda is event-driven. A file lands in S3, someone calls an API, or a timer fires, and your function springs into action.

reels.title: Pay only while it runs
reels.body: You pay per request plus the time your code runs, billed by the millisecond. An idle function costs nothing.

flashcards.back: Servers still exist, but AWS runs, patches and scales them. You only write the code.

flashcards.front: What can trigger a Lambda function?
flashcards.back: Events like an S3 upload, a schedule, or an API request, like the one that just loaded this lesson.

flashcards.front: How long can one invocation run?
flashcards.back: Up to 15 minutes. Longer jobs get split into steps or moved to another service.
Lambda scales automatically, running more copies of your function in parallel as requests grow.

quiz.q: What does AWS Lambda let you do?
quiz.why: Lambda is serverless compute: you bring the code, AWS runs it.

quiz.q: Which of these can trigger a Lambda function?
options: Only a manual click in the console
A new file uploaded to S3
quiz.why: Lambda is event-driven, and an S3 upload is a classic trigger.
You pay per request and for compute time, billed by the millisecond.

quiz.q: What's the longest a single Lambda invocation can run?
quiz.why: Each invocation can run for up to 15 minutes.

quiz.q: Traffic to your function suddenly doubles. What happens?
quiz.why: Lambda runs more copies of your function in parallel as requests grow.
